newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPALS -- slipping after payrolls.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPALS -- slipping after payrolls.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds slipped in early trade Friday, as concerns the Federal Reserve might have to tighten were reawakened by the latest economic data, which showed that while wages were flat, jobs rose sharply.
"You really can't tell, there's nothing trading at all," a trader said. "I would say bids are down a quarter of a point and offers are down an 0.1," he estimated.

While the market's softer tone, which mirrored losses in the Treasury bonds, was not enough to derail deals slated for next week, there was speculation that some buyers, who had been confident that the recent bullish tone was here to stay, might be tempted to take a few profits.
"You might see people saying I really ought to sell now, it could go down," the trader added.

And the latest data on payrolls, wages and personal income might only trigger a temporary halt in the market's climb. "I don't think there was anything to be alarmed about here, though we could see a little halt in the forward momentum. The freight train seems to be slowing down a little bit here," another trader said.
In Chicago futures markets, September municipal futures 11 ticks to 121-27/32. And September Treasury bonds 14 ticks to 116-10/32. The MOB spread stood at 172 ticks, down one tick from the close.
In the secondary market, volume slipped slightly to $1.275 billion, according to the Standard and Poor's Corp Blue List.
Actively traded issues included Delaware River Port Authority of Pennsylvania and New Jersey Revenues of 2026, which pay 5-1/2 percent, were bid at 101-1/4, unchanged.
Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority Massachusetts General Transportation bonds of 2024, which pay a 5.0 percent coupon, were bid at 5.34 percent, NET, up two basis points.

The U.S. economy kept adding jobs at a startling rate in July, when payrolls surged by 316,000, well above the consensus forecast for a gain of 193,000. The service sector added a strong 320,000 jobs.

However, economists saw few signs of inflation, as average earnings were flat at $12.23 an hour, surprising economists who had expected a 0.2 percent increase, while the workweek fell to 34.4 hours from 34.7.
These findings helped offset the slightly lower unemployment rate, which eased to 4.8 percent from 5.0 percent in June.

A Labor Department official said the July jobs data reflected the pattern of recent months, and cautioned against reading too much into one month's figures. Economists said they next will be closely watching retail sales reports for any signs that consumer spending was starting to increase.
June personal income climbed 0.6 percent, with spending rising 0.3 percent. Economists had looked for 0.4 percent rises in both categories.
